item.title: First they came for Ilhan Omar
item.description: Birthright citizenship is dumb. That's the point.
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

The Argument will be hosting a live election night watch party, with Nate Silver of Silver Bulletin and Galen Druke of GD Politics! Join us for reactions from some of the sharpest analysts in the business, plus guest appearances from other renowned experts as the night plays out.

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Jerusalem Demsas

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., wasn’t born here, but the Trump administration’s nascent attempt to strip her legal status is the best argument I can imagine for birthright citizenship.

Precisely because Omar is not a birthright citizen, her case shows us what a determined government can do when citizenship is contingent and contested. It can dig through your family history looking for a reason to declare that you were never really an American.

Birthright citizenship forecloses that kind of abuse. It offers a remarkably simple guarantee: You were born in the United States, so you are an American, and no one can take that away from you.

Omar came to the U.S. as a 12-year-old refugee from Somalia in 1995. She became a U.S. citizen at 17 in tandem with her father. And now, the Trump administration is looking to reverse all of that because Omar committed the crime of having bad takes — a charge that not a soul in the Trump administration could beat.

The case revolves around Omar’s birth year: An old Minnesota legislative biography listed her as born in 1981 rather than 1982, her official birth year. Her staff had the date corrected in 2019, saying it was an error, but Trump administration investigators are now examining whether Omar or her father intentionally lied about her age on immigration paperwork. If she was actually born in 1981, she would have been an adult when her father became a citizen in 2000, meaning she wouldn’t have automatically been granted citizenship alongside him.

None of this would be happening if Omar weren’t an outspoken progressive who has spent a decade as a vocal opponent of President Trump, launching inquiries into the administration’s controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operation in Minnesota and vowing to vote against giving a “single cent“ to ICE.

As the far right has become increasingly unhinged about Somali immigrants — Trump called them “garbage” four times in seven seconds at a Cabinet meeting last December — the administration has fixated on Omar’s citizenship: Trump has said we should “throw her the hell out of our country,“ and that she “could also go to jail.” Vice President JD Vance has said Omar “definitely committed immigration fraud“ and that he was working with White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller to figure out “remedies.”

Going after the citizenship status of your political opponents is, and I do not say this lightly, Nazi shit.

Hannah Arendt, who, like millions of Jews, was made stateless by the Nazis, argued in The Origins of Totalitarianism that the stateless person is worse off than a criminal because at least a criminal has rights. A stateless person is akin to Dred Scott, the African-American slave who sued for his freedom but was told by the Supreme Court that Black people could not be U.S. citizens. In the court’s view, they had “no rights which the white man was bound to respect.”

This is why the first part of the 14th Amendment — ratified a decade after the Dred Scott decision and the brutal Civil War that followed it — reads: “All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens...”

Birthright citizenship isn’t some quirk of English common law that we never got around to fixing. It’s the specific remedy we adopted when we watched how the government treated people who didn’t count as rights-bearing individuals. It works by taking the power to decide who belongs out of the government’s hands.

We already know how bad things can get without durable safeguards around citizenship. The first citizenship law that the Nazis passed a few months after Hitler took power in 1933 gave the regime power to revoke naturalizations and strip citizenship from Germans abroad. The first list issued under it named 33 people including regime critics like Kurt Tucholsky and social democratic political opponents. Albert Einstein was on the second such list, the novelist Thomas Mann was on a 1936 list, and Arendt was added in 1938. By 1945, there had been 359 lists including 39,006 names, and a 1941 decree had made every German Jew living abroad stateless.

Eighty years later, watching the U.S. government comb through a sitting congresswoman’s 26-year-old immigration file for a reason to deport her, I have no patience for engaging with the persecution of Ilhan Omar as if it’s an abstract debate about whether someone could ever be prosecuted for citizenship fraud. Trump officials have a history of arguing for their right to revoke citizenship — including birthright citizenship — on a wide variety of grounds.

Birthright citizenship may not protect Omar — or, for that matter, me (I was naturalized in high school when my dad became a citizen) — but it guarantees the rights of 284 million native-born Americans. The Supreme Court has held since 1967 that the government can never strip the status of birthright citizens. In June, the Court explicitly reaffirmed the citizenship of children born here to undocumented immigrants or people on temporary visas, rejecting Trump’s attempt to exclude them in an executive order he signed on his first day back in office.

Five weeks after the Court’s decision, the administration was back at it with orders attempting to make citizenship at birth turn on whether your parents have been designated terrorists or foreign-government employees.

Questions about birthright citizenship aren’t only coming from the far right. John Arnold, a big funder of serious evidence-based policy work (and whose organization, Arnold Ventures, is an investor in The Argument) posted a Venn diagram to Twitter last year: one circle for people who oppose birthright citizenship as policy, one for people who think the Constitution plainly requires it. He placed himself squarely in the intersection. Clive Crook, Bloomberg opinion columnist and former Economist deputy editor, argued that the Supreme Court was technically correct on the legal question while calling birthright citizenship “questionable at best.” Bill Maher derided birthright citizenship as “kind of crazy.”

Many other voices across the political spectrum have raised the prospect of eliminating birthright citizenship, usually by pointing out how unusual it is: Most rich countries don’t do it. They’re right that America is exceptional in this regard — but when have we been anything but?

The point of birthright citizenship is that it doesn’t care whether your parents are criminals or liars or whether they ever intended to stay in the country to begin with. It doesn’t even care about whether you’ll turn out to be the kind of person a sensible country would choose! It asks just one thing: Were you born here?

From a technocrat’s perspective, this is hardly optimal. Surely there is some set of criteria by which we could select for better and worse citizens. Maybe there is! But the question is whether we want the government to have that kind of power. The current one has told you what it thinks of Somalis and Muslims.

The virtue of birthright citizenship is that it is dumb on purpose. It gives the state almost nothing to decide when it comes to the citizenship of most of the polity. The question isn’t what rule a wise government would design; it’s what kind of guarantee prevents an unwise government from revoking fundamental rights.

Being a citizen doesn’t confer goodness or worth. Timothy McVeigh was just as much a citizen as Dolly Parton. The government had plenty of tools to ensure that McVeigh was punished for the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing: It tried and convicted him of murder, and it even executed him in accordance with the laws he was bound by.

What it could not do, at any point, was make him something other than an American.

Share

Midterm update

Lakshya Jain, our director of political data, uses data from The Argument’s polling operation to inform the Split Ticket 2026 House and Senate models. Here’s his update on the state of play this week:

Third-quarter fundraising updates are in, and unsurprisingly, Democrats remain commanding favorites to take back the House. Our model is more bullish for Democrats on several races than many experts are, and in a wave that continues to rise, even redder seats like Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District and Missouri’s 2nd have come onto the board as toss-ups. Meanwhile, in the Senate, the model gives Democrats a 64% chance of winning the majority — not a decisive likelihood, but a notable one.

These models update every day; bookmark this page to see the odds of each party taking the House and the Senate.

Top stories this week, by Milan Singh

In 2020, Joe Biden won Medicaid recipients by 19 points. In 2024, Donald Trump won the same group by 2 points. Then he signed a law subjecting many Medicaid recipients to work requirements. Now, as University of Michigan law professor writes, the Trump administration is trying to break its own law because it’s afraid those rules won’t strip enough people of their healthcare.

Some social conservatives have begun arguing that the sexual revolution of the 1960s and 1970s is responsible for the rape case unfolding at Cornell University — and many other social ills besides. Does that mean we should RETVRN to the good old days before birth control? does not think so! She points out that earlier social arrangements came with much more obvious downsides than their boosters acknowledge. She also notes that conservatives’ new obsession with the pleasures of married sex is itself unthinkable without the new norms they decry.

Anthropic invited The Argument’s and to its San Francisco offices for a two-day briefing with some of its top researchers. The researchers think that their pursuit of self-improving AI models will, at best, lead to the complete vaporization of our current social relations and, at worst, lead to human extinction. Are they crazy? Kelsey’s not entirely sure, but she thinks it’s probably time for the government to stop them regardless.

🌟Abundance Wins of the Week🌟

  • The Bureau of Land Management sold leases to nearly 200,000 acres of federal land in Nevada for geothermal energy, netting $4.83 million. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the permitting reform bill recently introduced in the Senate, includes legislation that would exempt some geothermal projects from National Environmental Policy Act review, putting the clean energy source on more even footing with oil and gas.

  • President Donald Trump signed a new executive order establishing a task force to issue recommendations on streamlining the permitting of manufactured housing. Currently there are several overlapping permitting and review processes for manufactured housing; the aim of this executive order is to eliminate redundant processes and ensure that agencies reciprocally recognize each other’s licenses and approvals.

  • The Nuclear Company announced a proposal for a new 6.6-gigawatt campus of up to six new nuclear reactors in Lewis County, Kentucky. That’s enough to power more than 5 million homes, according to the EIA. The hope is to begin construction in 2028, pending regulatory approval.

Subscribe now

Worth watching…

The Senate recently released the text of major permitting reform legislation, which among other things promises to make it much easier to build the high-voltage transmission necessary to facilitate renewable energy. But some environmental organizations are lukewarm-to-cold on the bill, arguing that it would also benefit fossil fuel companies. On this week’s podcast, and discuss whether elected Democrats should listen to the green groups or not. To the extent that Democrats believe their own campaign promises about affordability, maybe they shouldn’t.

The midterms are shaping up to be something between a blue wave and a blue tsunami. Polls, election models, and betting markets currently have Democrats favored to flip the House and (more narrowly) the Senate. But some Democratic nominees in key races, such as Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, are on track to underperform, while others, such as Adam Hamilton in Kansas, look like they might pull off upset wins in deep-red states. On Substack Live, The Argument’s and VoteHub’s were joined by Silver Bulletin’s to discuss how candidate quality might shape the battle for the Senate.

Many people who have worked at Anthropic and OpenAI are concerned that AI tools could pose catastrophic (or even existential) risks to humanity. In a Substack Live conversation, spoke with Hamza Chaudhry of the Future of Life Institute about how AI could supercharge existing threats posed by nuclear weapons and genetically engineered viruses.

What’s News with The Argument

The Argument recommends, by Milan Singh

Our editor-in-chief, , read Philip Roth’s The Human Stain and says she is “now a stan-for-life.” The novel is set in the summer of 1998, shortly after the Monica Lewinsky scandal broke, and the main character is also grappling with various scandals in his own personal life. “That’s as specific as I want to get because I’m spoiler-phobic,” she said, “but it’s really about the prudish style of American politics and whether true freedom from the life you’re handed means leaving it all behind.”

This week, “at the behest of a friend,” gender and culture fellow read the millennial British journalist Dolly Alderton’s memoir Everything I Know About Love. Initially dismissive of the book — “how interesting could it possibly be to read about the chaos of being confused, drunk, depressed, and in love in your 20s?” — Maibritt ended up coming around: “The best thing about Alderton’s writing is that she somehow manages to be completely earnest without ever taking herself too seriously.” May we all strive to do the same.

Staff writer recommended the video game Into the Breach, “one of the best roguelike games in recent years.” He’s a big fan of the roguelike genre — a type of video game where you must start from the beginning each time your character dies — with some of his favorites being Into the Breach, FTL, Balatro, Slay the Spire, and Hades. Editor wanted to add on Blue Prince as a standout in the genre.

Eli also had a spookier recommendation: “I was highly skeptical that Carrie needed a fourth screen adaptation when Mike Flanagan announced he was doing it, but the man can’t miss,” he told me.

Senior video producer finished Marcel Proust’s Swann’s Way and loved “how slow and deliberate the language was, and how his similes are so original and insightful.” He offered the following example, from the Lydia Davis translation: “Sometimes in the afternoon sky the moon would pass white as a cloud, furtive, lusterless, like an actress who does not have to perform yet and who, from the audience, in street clothes, watches the other actors for a moment, making herself inconspicuous, not wanting anyone to pay attention to her.”

recommends The New Yorker staff writer Ava Kofman’s new five-part narrative podcast series “The Journey”: “Come for the bizarre true crime saga, stay for the uncomfortable questions about the future of American surrogacy.”

When reached for comment, staff writer said that “weekly is just more often than I experience the culture, I’m sorry.”

item.title: What economists just don’t get about climate change
item.description: The case against cheap climate policy
item.content:encoded:
By Noah Kaufman

Economists working on climate change are used to being ignored. We often blame the political right for failing to recognize the benefits of climate actions and the political left for failing to recognize the costs. And both deserve some blame.

The Trump administration has gutted federal climate policy. Meanwhile, the Biden administration’s signature climate law sidelined the market-based measures, like carbon pricing, that economists have long recommended.

But we should also point our fingers at the mirror. The trouble is that economists and climate advocates are often talking past each other. Economic studies on climate policies tend to ask which policies cut the next ton of emissions most cheaply. But most climate policy advocates are after something else: system-level changes that will put the country (or, preferably, the world) on an entirely different path, where net greenhouse gas emissions bend toward zero over the coming decades.

Share

The case for costlier, system-level interventions stems from the physics of climate change. Carbon dioxide is a stock pollutant, meaning that a large share of it lingers in the atmosphere, causing global warming for centuries after it’s emitted. What determines how hot the planet gets is the total that accumulates over time.

The goal is not to reduce current emissions a little but instead to reduce future emissions a lot. The difference between these approaches would not matter much if cutting emissions a lot were just cutting emissions a little, many times over. But it usually isn’t. The cheapest way to reduce emissions in the near term and the cheapest way to transform energy systems over decades likely entail entirely different actions.

The problem, from the perspective of climate advocates, is that economic analyses don’t often come out in favor of systems-level interventions.

Consider the electricity system. Cheap emissions cuts can often come from switching from one fossil fuel generation source to a somewhat cleaner source — in particular from coal to natural gas. Around two-thirds of the considerable decarbonization of the U.S. power sector that occurred between 2005 and 2019 was caused by cheap gas replacing dirtier coal.

But that strategy only goes so far. These relatively easy emissions reductions are exhausted once the coal generation is gone and what’s left is gas-fired generation, and the long-lived infrastructure that remains will continue to be a major source of carbon dioxide; in other words, a policy that achieved substantial near-term decarbonization relatively cost-effectively did little to transform the power sector into a fully carbon-free system.

Deeper emissions reductions require a portfolio of carbon-free sources that can deliver power when and where it’s needed. From that perspective, the most cost-effective strategies in recent decades may have been early-stage investments in clean technologies, like solar and batteries, whose falling costs and improved performance are now making emissions reductions cheaper throughout the world.

This is old news for anyone familiar with decarbonization strategies. For decades, economists and other climate policy analysts have shown that the least-cost path to deep decarbonization often means paying for some high-cost, slow-to-move options early — like clean steel production or carbon-free jet fuel — because skipping them makes the long-run target more expensive or simply unreachable.

This insight shaped the design of measures within Joe Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act and Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, which focused as much on long-term transformation as on immediate emissions cuts. Yet the cost figures that dominate policy evaluations and public debates still focus on the near-term costs of reducing the next ton of emissions.

It’s time for that to change.

Cost-effective climate actions aren’t always cheap

Climate policies are commonly assessed by comparing them with a carbon price. Carbon prices encourage emissions cuts from wherever and however they can be achieved at a relatively low cost, so nearly any other policy looks expensive compared with them.

Back to the example of coal-to-gas shifting, a coal power plant emits roughly one metric ton of CO2 per megawatt-hour, about double a natural gas plant’s half-ton, so a carbon price raises the cost of running a coal plant more than it raises the cost of a natural gas plant. Even a small carbon price is often enough to flip the order in which grid operators dispatch generators to serve customers at the lowest cost, so the higher-emitting coal plants run less, and the government brings in revenue in the process.

However, carbon prices are limited tools for driving large emissions cuts cost-effectively. Vehicle emissions are a good illustration. Some can be cut cheaply from the tailpipe: Tightening fuel-economy standards wrings more miles from each gallon, and a modest carbon price nudges people to drive a bit less, delivering real but small reductions.

But large-scale vehicle emissions reductions are a different project that requires getting Americans to switch from internal combustion engine vehicles to electric or other alternative-fuel vehicles.

Subscribe now

In principle, a carbon price could drive that shift, too, by raising gasoline and diesel prices so high that drivers switch to EVs. But, in addition to the political challenges of imposing high carbon prices, that approach is likely to cost more than other strategies. Alternatives could rely somewhat less on gasoline price hikes and somewhat more on policies like zero-emission vehicle standards or “feebates” that encourage the purchase of cleaner vehicles.

To see why, imagine two extremes. In the first, EVs are near-perfect substitutes for gasoline vehicles, identical to drivers in virtually every way. Then, a zero-emission vehicle standard that gradually mandates more EV sales costs almost nothing, because buyers are indifferent. In contrast, a carbon price could shift those new-car decisions only by jacking up gasoline prices for the entire existing fleet, taxing millions of drivers who own gasoline-powered cars they won’t replace for years, all to influence the far smaller group choosing a new vehicle today.

In the second extreme, there is no viable alternative to the gasoline engine at all. Now the standard would be impossible to meet, while the carbon price would at least capture the changes from nudging people to drive less and to buy more efficient vehicles.

Reality sits in between these two extremes, which is why both tools are useful. But the closer EVs come to substituting for gasoline cars, the more cost-effective standards become as a tool for achieving large emissions reductions.

A 2022 study of Canada’s vehicle market bears this out. It found the cheapest strategy capable of achieving the country’s vehicle emissions goals involved a zero-emission vehicle standard, even though the costs of this policy were estimated at hundreds of dollars per ton. Comparing that with the low costs of Canada’s carbon price would mislead, since the carbon price would not have delivered the same transformation of the fleet. (Canada got rid of its carbon price on vehicle emissions last year.)

Misleading policy verdicts

To weigh the costs of a climate policy against its benefits, you need a way to value those benefits: a dollar figure for the damage avoided by keeping the next ton of carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere. In theory, that enables a comparison of the harm caused by a ton of emissions with the cost of preventing that ton — and therefore a verdict on whether the policy in question is worth doing.

The trouble is that real-world calculations of this figure — referred to as the social cost of carbon — are not meaningful estimates of the benefits of reducing emissions. While analyses of the harms climate change will cause and how people will adapt to them are valuable, aggregated estimates of global climate damages over centuries lie far beyond the capabilities of our modeling tools.

First, the models put dollar figures on the harms economists know how to measure, like how mortality rates and energy bills rise as the planet warms, and leave out the rest, with no way of knowing whether what they have captured is one-tenth of the total damage or most of it.

Second, they use historical data as a guide for how people will adapt to a climate with no precedent in human history, even though economists have long recognized, in other settings, that the empirical relationships estimated under the conditions we have observed are a poor guide to conditions we have not.

Third, analysts make a series of moral judgments about how much to value people’s well-being decades or centuries from now, and how much weight to give to avoiding future risks and the uneven distribution of harms.

To produce a single estimate of total climate damages, the models have to settle these difficult questions one way or another. They do so in ways that keep the math manageable — not because economics can say which values are the right ones.

The result is not a fuzzy estimate of something real. It is a precise estimate of something the method cannot actually produce. It is a bit like gauging the relative size of Greenland from a flat map, except that here we have little sense of the size or the direction of the distortion.

It’s expensive to do hard things.

Subscribe now

The upshot is that while weighing the potential costs and benefits of climate measures is essential to sound policy, empirical estimates are used in misleading ways. The near-term costs of transformational policies are compared with the costs of more incremental policies like a carbon price, or against a social cost of carbon, as if these are meaningful comparisons. They usually aren’t.

Consider the example John Thomason’s recent essay offers on renewable portfolio standards (RPS), policies many states use to require that a gradually rising share of electricity come from resources like wind and solar. He cites a prominent study finding RPS costs $86 to $211 per ton of avoided emissions and contrasts that with the much lower costs of the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI), a power-sector-carbon-pricing policy that operates across northeastern states.

Indeed, even at their highest levels in the history of the policy, recent RGGI carbon prices around $35 per ton are a bargain for CO2 reductions (and the costs of the policy are smaller once the productive use of revenue is considered). That’s by design: RGGI’s rules are meant to keep prices at levels that cause only small increases in electricity rates. But it also means the carbon prices cannot rise high enough to encourage much additional carbon-free generation.

A $35-per-ton carbon price adds only 1 or 2 cents per kilowatt-hour to the costs of burning natural gas, far short of the incentive needed to encourage clean electricity sources to grow at scale in the region.

So, especially in states with no remaining coal to shift away from, RGGI is an instrument that can efficiently reduce emissions a little, but it cannot reduce emissions a lot. One reason RPS policies are more expensive is that they are trying to do the harder thing — build carbon-free generation — rather than the easier changes that RGGI can provoke.

Now, imagine you are a policymaker in a New England state where RGGI, an RPS, and a host of other clean energy measures operate. You want your state to be a climate leader, but you do not currently have a policy portfolio that is aligned with your ambitious long-term emissions goals, and high electricity prices leave little room to add climate policies without noticeable economic trade-offs. You badly need guidance on how to build a cost-effective strategy from here.

In the power sector, that means understanding the trade-offs among measures that could bring on more solar, wind, batteries, and nuclear — or transmission and pipelines to access low-cost energy from neighboring regions. A backward-looking comparison of RGGI and the RPS answers a different question from the one you are asking.

An economics of humility

None of this excuses the all-too-common practice of ignoring the costs and trade-offs of climate actions. More careful thinking about costs and benefits could help avoid policy blunders, like the reflex to block fossil fuel production wherever possible, even when doing so is expensive and barely affects global emissions, because the production simply moves elsewhere.

Subscribe now

This instinct is driving some of the opposition to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, recently introduced in Congress. That permitting reform bill would speed the build-out of clean energy that deep decarbonization requires, but because it would also make fossil fuel infrastructure easier to build, parts of the climate movement have lined up against it. Fighting a bill that would help the climate because it also helps fossil fuels, rather than working to improve it, is just the kind of mistake that weighing costs against benefits helps to prevent.

But if the goal is to get climate advocates to weigh costs and benefits, scolding them for ignoring economic analysis may be counterproductive. Economists should press for more cost-benefit thinking from a place of humility about what we can and cannot deliver.

While economists will and should continue to analyze the near-term costs of incremental changes, they should also build tools that better capture the factors that large-scale emissions reductions depend on. On this front, many economists are already at work.

For example, one recent study in a top economics journal shows that the cost-effectiveness of electric vehicle subsidies improves dramatically once the dynamic effects of accelerated innovation are taken into account (though EV subsidies still cost far more than subsidies for wind), and that the cost-effectiveness of energy efficiency programs depends heavily on how clean the regional electricity grid is.

Perhaps more importantly, a humbler approach to encouraging more cost-benefit thinking would mean showing up to policy debates as contributors rather than as arbiters handing down verdicts. For reasonable policies with the potential to make genuine progress on the parts of the problem that actually require transformation — like getting oil out of vehicles or cutting natural gas use in electricity and heating — economists should skip the ritual comparisons to a carbon price or the social cost of carbon, which they may have previously used to brand policies as inefficient.

For a proposed clean vehicle standard, for instance, acting as a contributor instead of an arbiter means helping to improve the design with flexibility measures that reduce compliance costs, analyzing how it will affect vehicle and fuel prices, and flagging unintended consequences, like distortions that could result from counting different fuels as clean or dirty.

Economic tools can produce genuinely useful information to help policymakers weigh the costs and benefits of cutting emissions. What they cannot produce are comprehensive estimates, or anything close, of the costs and benefits that policymakers actually care about. We should be far more transparent about those limitations.

Counterintuitively, scaling back the ambition of our analysis may be what finally makes it useful.

item.title: My weekend with the “sex-realist” feminists
item.content:encoded:
By Maibritt Henkel

“What would it take to create a world in which every baby is welcome, without this coming at the cost of his or her mother’s personhood?”

This was the question that Mary Harrington, contributing editor at UnHerd and self-described “reactionary feminist,” asked at the outset of the 2026 Women’s Convention, a three-day conference I attended last month in Rochester, New York. Harrington and I disagree on just about everything, but her question struck me as a good one. What could be more true to my own liberal politics than ensuring the dignity and well-being of women who choose to have children?

The conference was co-hosted by the “sex-realist” publication Fairer Disputations and the anti-abortion advocacy group Feminists Choosing Life of New York. Like Harrington, most of the 200 women in attendance were white, married, and Christian. I met a publicist from Colorado, a chaplain living in Texas, and a homeschooling mother of four from New Jersey. All of them gave me the impression that they could breastfeed and debate Aristotle at the same time.

No one I spoke to was enthusiastic about Donald Trump (or the Democratic Party). Several expressed concern about the growing threat of misogyny on the right. A gaggle of conservative college women from Michigan told me they worried about their male classmates who joked about repealing the 19th Amendment. When guest speaker Helen Roy, a popular Catholic Substacker, mentioned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth onstage, the auditorium collectively groaned.

Share

One morning, I carpooled to the conference venue, a Tudor Revival mansion in a leafy part of town, with a group of chatty ladies in a minivan. If they were put off by my press badge and libbed-out vibe, it didn’t show.

And yet, however friendly I found this congregation, however well-read and well-dressed, improving the material lives of mothers was not what they wanted to talk about.

The presentations and panels I attended, as well as the many conversations I had over lunch and tea and cake, seemed gravitationally pulled away from childcare policies and toward the countless evils of liberal feminism: hookup culture, pornography, abortion, birth control, in vitro fertilization, surrogacy — to name just a few.

I am not against debating any of these issues, but the women I met in Rochester did not convince me that they ought to be the focus of a bipartisan, pro-family agenda. Much more could be accomplished with old-fashioned welfare policies, such as generous parental leave standards and child allowances, because such policies recognize both the unique challenges faced by mothers and the increasingly gender-neutral realities of caring for children in America.

These are realities that the assembled women seemed to be living out in their own egalitarian marriages, despite their obsession with sex differences. (Even among conservatives, time spent caring for children has risen fastest among fathers, not mothers.)

Ultimately, I left the Women’s Convention more certain than ever that cracking down on overachieving girlbosses who have premarital sex, freeze their eggs, and watch porn is not how you help American parents.

No one hates children. Please be serious.

Despite the country’s wealth, having kids in America is a daunting proposition. There is no federal law guaranteeing paid family leave, childcare is absurdly expensive, and employees are expected to log more annual hours than in most other wealthy nations. There really are big professional and personal trade-offs associated with raising children, especially for women.

The left and right agree that having a family should be easier. But despite the conferencegoers’ disdain for MAGA, their answer to the question of what has gone wrong in American family life is very similar to one offered by the second Trump administration: Some version of liberal or second-wave feminism is to blame.

Vice President JD Vance has long attributed the falling birth rate to an “anti-child” ideology propagated by a managerial class of liberal elites. In 2022, shortly after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, he tweeted: “If your worldview tells you that it’s bad for women to become mothers but liberating for them to work 90 hours a week in a cubicle at the New York Times or Goldman Sachs, you’ve been had.”

This past January, Vance gave a speech at the 2026 March for Life, saying, “Today, the far left in this country tells our young people that marriage and children are obstacles ... that life itself is a burden.”

It’s a convenient political position: As long as the problem is primarily cultural rather than economic, it doesn’t take much to look like you’re solving it. Announcing that you have a fourth kid on the way is enough to make it seem like you are bravely defeating the cat ladies who cowed everyone else into childlessness.

Unlike the vice president, the Rochester women seem genuinely interested in solving the problem. But here is what you have to understand about them: They care a lot about biology. Their central claim is that there are immutable differences between the sexes that social gender identity cannot change — hence the label “sex-realist” feminism.

You cannot just “identify” as a woman, you simply are a woman by virtue of your biology. To be a woman, according to the mission statement of Fairer Disputations, is to be “a person whose body is organized according to the tremendous potential to grow another human being within.”

From this metaphysical perspective, women who do not have biological children — such as lesbians, transgender women, single girlbosses — challenge the very thing that makes women distinct from men, the thing that ought to afford them distinct protections and privileges.

This is the idea that united every headline speaker at the convention, and it’s also the one that puts their intellectual movement at odds with the central claim of liberal feminism: that no one’s lot in life should be determined by their sex. The sex-realist writers who presented at the convention — including Louise Perry, author of The Case Against the Sexual Revolution, and Leah Libresco Sargeant, editorial director at the Institute for Progress (as well as a contributor to The Argument) — share a suspicion of what they consider to be “transhumanist” interventions into the natural female body.

In her welcoming address, legal scholar Erika Bachiochi accused “the regnant form of feminism” (her pejorative for the second wave) of assuming “a series of technological incursions into the body of a young woman such that she can become the equal of a man.” These incursions include “a lifetime on the contraceptive pill, abortion at the ready, the availability of egg-freezing, and other reproductive technologies.”

The upshot is that women who opt into these technologies (not to mention those who commit the unspeakable offense of being trans) have made life worse for all the women who refused them. Like a worker crossing the picket line, the childless corporate lawyer undermined the collective bargaining power of normal women who wanted normal things, such as raising a big family.

When motherhood is understood as a personal choice, rather than an unavoidable fact of life, institutions are under less pressure to accommodate mothers. If women want to make their lives harder by getting pregnant, that’s on them! As a 29-year-old from Seattle described it to me: “Liberal feminism is the new patriarchy. It tells women what to do with their bodies: work all the time and don’t have kids.”

What is clever about this argument is that it draws on pro-choice logic: A liberal society should protect the rights of women who choose to forgo contraception and artificial reproductive technology.

Around 1 in 5 Americans identify as Catholic and are, in theory, bound by church doctrine, which opposes most human intervention in reproduction. Evangelical Protestants, who make up around 23% of the population, tend to hold a similar set of beliefs. That a sizable number of women would feel defensive about their right to defy what has become increasingly normalized by secular society makes sense.

But the case being built at the Women’s Convention went well beyond religious freedom. The main charge against liberal feminism wasn’t that it had served some women and neglected others — it was that it had done an injustice to all women, convincing them that they had to change their bodies and disavow childbearing to be free. In this framing, the freedom to have an abortion or get an IUD isn’t freedom at all; it is a kind of payoff from a society that doesn’t want women to live as women.

Now, there are countless objections to be made against biological essentialism. For one, it sets up trans individuals as the ultimate threat to cisgender women, which, irrespective of your stance on puberty blockers, is simply a cruel and ludicrous war to wage.

It also sidelines the women who would like to get pregnant but can’t, either because they are infertile, as roughly 10% of American women between the ages of 15 and 44 are, or because they know that pregnancy might cost them their lives.

Then, of course, there is the possibility that a woman might not want to be a mother.

In reality, most Americans want to become parents — even, and perhaps especially, the high-powered career woman whose norms are being blamed for the downfall of Western civilization. Among American millennials, 75% of college-educated women born in the early 1980s married and became parents by 40. For non-college women, that number was 68.1%.

Whatever campaign is happening against traditional family values on progressive college campuses, it is not a very effective one.

As Jordan McGillis and Cathy Reisenwitz recently wrote for The Argument, family formation primarily poses a challenge for Americans without college degrees, largely due to the declining standing of working-class men. Today, it is much harder for non-college women to find husbands who have the relative earning power of their fathers or grandfathers, let alone the commitment to intensive fatherhood that is fast becoming the modern norm.

The Women’s Convention’s accusation against liberal feminism was that it pushed women to meet traditionally masculine standards, “in the bedroom and in the marketplace.” Instead of treating women as defective men, these women argue, society should accommodate women’s unaltered bodies.

In the abstract, that’s all fine and well (although I didn’t see much leg hair at the conference).

But among Americans in the lower half of the income distribution, the problem is not that women are being forced to pursue masculine ideals that they can’t meet. It’s that men can’t meet the masculine ideals of 50 years ago because modern economic conditions favor a very different model of marriage (an egalitarian model that Americans say they prefer anyway).

The mismatch in the non-college marriage market is a different beast entirely from elite women opting out of motherhood because Gloria Steinem convinced them children were deadweight. It is also one that the “sex realism” espoused at the Women’s Convention provides no solution for.

Men and women can change

I have never been pregnant or given birth. And if I do, I imagine that I will want everyone to give me a lot of credit for having done those things — more credit than my co-parent who did neither.

The realities of reproduction are, however, not the same as the realities of caregiving. While mothers typically play a distinct parenting role for the duration of pregnancy and, to a lesser extent, breastfeeding, this period of time is then followed by a lifetime of parental obligations that do not require this or that reproductive organ.

Sex-realist feminism isn’t particularly interested in that distinction. The view is basically that, if you have a uterus, your entire life, from the day you are born to the day you die, is defined by this physiological trait.

“But not in a bad way!” the sex realists will tell you. “Your uterus is a gift!”

The only thing is, I would quite like my uterus to not determine who picks up the kids from school or changes their diapers or puts them to bed at night. I also don’t want it to determine who in my marriage makes more money or gets to attend fun conferences.

The good news is, I don’t actually think the Women’s Convention participants want this either. Almost all of them went to college, many of them have law degrees, and an astounding number of them have Substack followings that put many of us liberal feminist writers to shame.

They were also open about the fact that they have husbands looking after their three or four children for the weekend. When I told them that where I come from (Denmark), fathers on average take 11 weeks of parental leave, compared to just one week or less in the U.S., they were approving.

Some social conservatives have started to blame liberal elites for disparaging traditional family life in public while privately living what look like traditional values: marrying, having children, and settling down. But this critique cuts both ways. Highly educated conservatives, including Vance and the women I hung out with in Rochester — who can quote Aquinas off the cuff and write books in their sleep — seem happy to practice gender egalitarianism in their private lives, as long as they don’t have to preach it as a cultural message.

But they should preach it. I understand why some of these women were frustrated to have three kids in their 20s while their childless female peers from law school zoomed up the corporate ladder. But if the traditional male breadwinner-female caregiver household — where men outearn women and women out-parent men — is the only kind of marriage our biology allows for, the future of the American family looks bleak.

On the other hand, if we assume gender roles are malleable, then a whole world of opportunity opens up. This does not necessarily mean promoting a culture of “radical autonomy” or “anti-child ideology.” On the contrary. It means making a “family-first” life possible for more people — not just women in heterosexual marriages with biological children.

The first injustice of several listed in the Declaration of Interdependence, the conference’s de facto manifesto, states that it is “unjust for ... society to champion those who are unencumbered by familial responsibilities as the standard bearers of equality and civic and economic participation.” Hear, hear.

Again, this part of the message clearly has cross-ideological appeal. The leftist theorist Nancy Fraser argued for something very similar in her 2013 book Fortunes of Feminism: institutions should “welcome human beings who can give birth and who often care for relatives and friends, treating them not as exceptions, but as ideal-typical participants.”

Unlike the sex realists, Fraser is explicit that men and women bear equal caregiving responsibilities. For her, biological realities are only as limiting as the political system allows.

Fraser’s position is that men should lead the charge on changing norms around parenting. Precisely because they don’t face discrimination for the biological fact of pregnancy, men are the ones who should be applying pressure on employers by taking paternity leave and clocking out early to attend ballet recitals. That pressure creates space for women to pursue both vocational fulfillment and family life without undue sacrifice.

But biologically fixed gender roles get in the way of this project. By the logic of sex realism, it is always women who are at fault. You can’t very well blame men for not taking on the burdens of childcare if they’re just following their reproductive destinies. You can only blame the girlboss with frozen eggs for shirking hers.
